function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
They cover:

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node 18 image for the app |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deployment manifest (2 replicas) |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Service manifest (ClusterIP) |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | GitHub Actions workflow that builds & pushes the image on every push to `main` |

> **NOTE** – The repository already contains a `package.json`, `app.js`, etc.  
> If your actual source layout differs, adjust the paths accordingly.

---

## 1. Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image: official Node 18 Alpine (small footprint)
FROM node:18-alpine

# Metadata
LABEL maintainer="ZelarHQ <support@zelarhq.com>"

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy only the dependency descriptors first
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official Alpine‑based Node image → small size.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * Exposes port 3000 (the default for many Node/Express apps).  
> * Keeps the image lean by copying `package*.json` first and installing before the rest of the code.

---

## 2. Kubernetes Manifests

Create a folder called `k8s` (or any name you prefer) and place the two YAML files there.

### 2.1 `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: docker.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
```

### 2.2 `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # External port exposed by the service
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment creates 2 replicas of the pod.  
> * Service exposes the pods internally via port 80 (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create the directory `.github/workflows/` (if it doesn’t exist) and add the following file:

### `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # 1️⃣ Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout repository
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # 2️⃣ Set up Docker Buildx (multi‑platform builder)
      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      # 3️⃣ Log in to Docker Hub
      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      # 4️⃣ Build & push the image
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: docker.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Secrets required**  
> * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username.  
> * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub personal access token (recommended over password).  
> Add them under **Settings → Secrets → Actions** in your GitHub repo.

---

## 4. Add, Commit & Push

Once you’ve added the files to the repo locally, run:

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> The GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the push, build the image, and push it to Docker Hub.

---

## 5. Quick sanity check

After pushing, verify:

1. **Docker image** – `docker pull docker.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest` (should succeed).  
2. **Kubernetes** – `kubectl apply -f k8s/` (apply the manifests).  
3. **Service** – `kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service` (should show ClusterIP).  

If you’re running locally, you can test the container directly:

```bash
docker run -p 3000:3000 docker.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

Open `http://localhost:3000` to see your app.

---

### TL;DR

| Step | Command |
|------|---------|
| Clone repo | `git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` |
| Add files | `git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml` |
| Commit | `git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, CI"` |
| Push | `git push origin main` |

That’s it! 🎉 If you hit any snags (e.g., missing `app.js`, different port), tweak the Dockerfile/K8s YAML accordingly. Happy deploying!
